purpose: Concise English subtitles translated against each Korean cue, not English speech timing.

cues.text: Think of leaving the shrine in Breath of the Wild.
You see a vast landscape, then step into it yourself.
Admiring scenery is different from feeling you can go there.
Let's explore what to show players when a game begins.
Not menu layouts, but the first scene the player controls.
That first scene promises the experience this game will offer.
Somewhere to explore,
or, in a mystery, a clue worth investigating.
But if explanations come before that promise,
you arrive for adventure and get employee orientation.
It's not whether you explain, but what players experience first.
Compare two openings: one explains the setting and controls first.
The other first shows the hero and a nearby destination.
We're comparing opening priorities, not features.
Either way, players should see what to expect from this game.
Before decorating that first screen, decide what it should make them feel.
Let's return to the Shrine of Resurrection.
Link wakes, gets the Sheikah Slate, and opens the way outside.
There are voice cues and control instructions, too.
Breath of the Wild does give you instructions.
Notice how it offers something to try, even in an unfamiliar space.
In the first playable scene, the character and surroundings
must form a readable relationship. Where am I?
What looks worth approaching? Those come first.
You can approach an object without knowing the world's history.
Separate understanding the setting from knowing what to do,
and the opening asks less of players all at once.
Keep the hero, the exit,
and the object. Change only the framing: an unclear layout versus
one that guides the eye from the hero to the object and exit.
Guidance doesn't just mean adding arrows.
Can the framing alone suggest what to do next? That's a design question.
On the Great Plateau, distant terrain or buildings may catch your interest.
Before deciding where to walk, notice what catches your eye.
Breath of the Wild has quest guidance, too. But beyond that,
how does something in the landscape become a place you want to reach?
A wider view doesn't always make the direction clearer.
If everything has equal emphasis, where should you look first?
Size, contrast, and empty space can create an order of attention.
Rather than reveal the whole route, choose what first draws the eye.
On the same terrain, compare competing focal points
with a view that singles out one first point of interest.
We're not adding destinations or changing the map.
If everything looks important, the whole screen is raising its hand.
Designing that first scene also means deciding what not to emphasize.
Watch how you notice and pick up a nearby item on the Plateau.
Even without a big battle, looking around and finding something is an experience.
Focus less on the item mechanic and more on its role in the opening.
It suggests a world that invites you to look around.
The first action isn't just a controls check. Is this a game about observing,
avoiding danger, or making choices? The player can learn that by doing.
Demand too many actions at once, and what players learned may become unclear.
First choose the one action you want them to experience here.
In the same space, compare many instructions appearing at once
with inviting players to inspect one nearby object first.
This shows how the scope of their first attempt changes.
A simple beginning doesn't mean the whole game must be simple.
Does a deep game need to throw players straight into the deep end?
Think about how you ease them in.
In the Magnesis shrine, moving metal plates opens a path.
It doesn't just announce a new ability.
You see what changes when you use it.
Don't just watch the object moving.
Notice how that movement connects to the route ahead.
After an interaction, players need a sign that it worked.
If nothing seems to change, they may press the button again instead of moving on.
Good feedback isn't just a flash of light.
The link between your action and the world's change should be clear,
and that change should give you a reason to continue.
Keep the button and door. Compare an off-screen result with a view
that shows the door opening. It's about readable results, not switch code.
If the result must be off-screen, sound or a brief camera cue can help.
One frame need not show everything.
The key is a clear connection between cause and effect.
As you explore the Great Plateau, new problems like cold appear.
You check temperature and status, then consider clothing or food effects.
This comes later than the first playable scene. The learning begun there
develops into another experience when players meet a new danger.
An opening needn't be safe. Some games need a dangerous or unsettling start.
But what players understand after failing matters.
Recognizing a failure's cause and changing your approach
isn't the same as being hurt for no clear reason. Whatever the difficulty,
check the visual clues that explain the danger.
With the same hazard, one version hides its cause;
the other shows how the danger zone relates to the change in status.
We're not removing difficulty, but making its cause readable.
If getting back to another attempt takes too long, early learning becomes a chore.
Design both the danger cues and the path back after failure.
The Old Man offers guidance and dialogue,
and there's a goal for leaving the Great Plateau.
Normally, you finish four shrines, get the paraglider, and leave for the next area.
So calling this an opening with no explanations or restrictions misses the point.
Guidance and exploration exist together.
When choosing opening information,
separate what's needed to act now from what's needed later.
It may not be wrong information, just too much arriving before there's a use for it.
Some scenes need an explanation just to make the goal clear.
Don't just cut instructions.
Ask whether they answer the player's question right now.
Keep the information the same, and change only when it's given.
Compare showing it all at the start
with giving relevant guidance after the first action.
In a story-driven game, opening dialogue may be the core experience.
It's not bad cutscenes versus good interaction.
Ask whether what you're showing starts this game's experience.
Gliding off the Plateau lets you explore the world you've seen in a new way.
The opening's actions carry into the adventure ahead.
Don't judge an opening only by how good its first screen looks.
Does the expectation it creates carry into the next scene?
Ask three questions about your first scene: what should players see first?
What should they try? Why should the result make them want to continue?
The advice about the first three minutes isn't a timer for every game.
Treat it as a question: when does the core experience begin?
Rushing the presentation isn't the point.
Finally, compare a start that stalls after its first goal
with one whose result reveals a new point of interest.
Where a scene ends and what it leaves behind can change the reason to act next.
A game's first scene isn't a manual explaining everything.
It's an invitation to try. Rather than list everything you want to teach,
design the experience you're inviting players into.
